The '''Medog Hydropower Station''' ({{lang-zh|墨脱水电站}})<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-12-26 |title=不顾印度孟加拉反对 准雅鲁藏布江水电站动工 |url=https://www.enanyang.my/%E5%9B%BD%E9%99%85/%E4%B8%8D%E9%A1%BE%E5%8D%B0%E5%BA%A6%E5%AD%9F%E5%8A%A0%E6%8B%89%E5%8F%8D%E5%AF%B9-%E5%87%86%E9%9B%85%E9%B2%81%E8%97%8F%E5%B8%83%E6%B1%9F%E6%B0%B4%E7%94%B5%E7%AB%99%E5%8A%A8%E5%B7%A5 |access-date=2024-12-28 |website=www.enanyang.my |language=zh-hans}}</ref> or '''Motuo Hydropower Station'''<ref>{{Cite news |last1=May |first1=Tiffany |last2=Qian |first2=Isabelle |last3=Raj |first3=Suhasini |date=2025-01-27 |title=China's Large and Mysterious Dam Project Is Alarming Neighbors and Experts |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/01/27/world/asia/china-tibet-dam-india.html |access-date=2025-02-02 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> is a planned 60,000 [[Watt|megawatt]] (MW) [[Run-of-the-river hydroelectricity|run-of-the-river]] [[Hydroelectricity|hydroelectric dam project]] on a single stretch or valley of a river under development on the [[Yarlung Tsangpo|Yarlung Tsangpo river]] in [[Tibet Autonomous Region]], China. It is of four cascade dams across the Yarlung Tsangpo River and five separate power stations<ref>{{Cite web |title= How China is building the $167 billion mega dam  |url=https://in.video.search.yahoo.com/video/play;_ylt=AwrKBUVkuGJqAnwbFwjmHAx.;_ylu=c2VjA3NyBHNsawN2aWQEZ3BvcwMx?p=how+china+is+building+dam+next+generation&vid=0d02a1795d75c132568ae3428b2bd752&turl=https%3A%2F%2Ftse1.mm.bing.net%2Fth%3Fid%3DOVF.%252fDQO%252fLhdIwmgaLJ9ima5Nw%26pid%3DApi%26h%3D360%26w%3D480%26c%3D7%26rs%3D1&rurl=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.youtube.com%2Fwatch%3Fv%3DlU7_g_XRCwE&tit=%3Cb%3EHow%3C%2Fb%3E+%3Cb%3EChina%3C%2Fb%3E+%3Cb%3EIs%3C%2Fb%3E+%3Cb%3EBuilding%3C%2Fb%3E+the+%24167+Billion+Mega+%3Cb%3EDam%3C%2Fb%3E+That+Will+Triple+Three+Gorges+Power&c=0&sigr=0jVle3HIWOPM&sigt=zOonkBA6_T_n&sigi=H0iGFAk3PhDq&fr2=p%3As%2Cv%3Av&h=360&w=480&l=927&age=1784822759&fr=mcafee&type=E210IN1586G0&tt=b |access-date=23 July 2026 |website=Next Gen Production}}</ref>  Upon completion, it will become the [[List of largest hydroelectric power stations|world's largest hydropower facility]],<ref name=":0a">{{Cite web |last=刘小卓 |title=Premier announces construction of Yarlung Zangbo hydropower project |url=https://www.chinadaily.com.cn/a/202507/19/WS687b6e94a310ad07b5d90d42.html |access-date=2025-07-21 |website=www.chinadaily.com.cn}}</ref><ref name=":1a">{{Cite news |last=Master |first=Farah |last2=Shen |first2=Samuel |last3=Master |first3=Farah |date=2025-07-21 |title=China embarks on world's largest hydropower dam, capital markets cheer |url=https://www.reuters.com/sustainability/climate-energy/china-embarks-worlds-largest-hydropower-dam-capital-markets-cheer-2025-07-21/ |access-date=2025-07-21 |work=Reuters |language=en}}</ref> with an anticipated annual power generation capacity of 10.8 PJ or 300 billion [[kilowatt-hour]]s—triple that of the [[Three Gorges Dam]]. The [[Government of China|Chinese government]] authorized the dam's construction in December 2024, with an estimated investment exceeding 1 trillion [[Renminbi|yuan]] (approximately [[United States dollar|US$]]137 billion).<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |date=27 December 2024 |title=China approves construction of mega-dam in Tibet |url=https://www.rfa.org/english/tibet/2024/12/27/tibet-china-approves-mega-dam-construction/ |access-date=27 December 2024 |work=[[Radio Free Asia]]}}</ref> Construction officially began on 19 July 2025.<ref name="reuters-20250721" /> The project is intended to be developed as a single-phase installation, with commercial operations planned for 2033.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last= |date=2023-08-29 |title=Power plant profile: Medog Project, China |url=https://www.power-technology.com/marketdata/power-plant-profile-medog-project-china/ |access-date=2024-12-28 |website=Power Technology |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Location ==
The facility is planned to be constructed in [[Mêdog County|Medog County]] within the [[Nyingchi|Nyingtri Prefecture]], situated near the [[India]]n border state of [[Arunachal Pradesh]]. It is the lower section of Yarlung Tsangpo, which originates in [[Geography of Tibet|western Tibet]]'s glacial regions. This watercourse continues into India as the [[Brahmaputra River]] and into [[Bangladesh]] as the [[Jamuna River (Bangladesh)|Jamuna River]], serving as a crucial water source for these regions.<ref name=":0" />

== Overview ==
The Medog Hydropower Station represents part of China's broader hydroelectric development strategy in [[Tibet]]. Since 2000, China has initiated or proposed 193 hydropower projects in the region, with approximately 60% still in planning or preparatory phases. Construction approval was granted in December 2024, with construction officially commencing on 19 July 2025.<ref name="reuters-20250721">{{cite web |last1=Master |first1=Farah |last2=Shen |first2=Samuel |url=https://www.reuters.com/sustainability/climate-energy/china-embarks-worlds-largest-hydropower-dam-capital-markets-cheer-2025-07-21/ |title=China embarks on world's largest hydropower dam, capital markets cheer |work=[[Reuters]] |date=2025-07-21 |access-date=2025-07-21}}</ref> The Chinese government has not yet released comprehensive environmental impact assessments or detailed implementation plans for the project.<ref name=":0" />

The project is wholly owned and developed by [[Power Construction Corporation of China]] (PowerChina), a state-owned construction enterprise. Commercial operations are planned to begin in 2033. With a projected investment more than quadruple that of the Three Gorges Dam (which cost 250 billion yuan), the Medog Hydropower Station represents one of China's most ambitious infrastructure projects and one of the most expensive infrastructure projects in history. The facility's planned annual power output of 300 billion kilowatt-hours would establish it as the world's most productive hydroelectric installation, significantly surpassing current records.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />

The project intends to harness a 2,000-meter river elevation drop within a 50-kilometer stretch nicknamed "the Great Bend",<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-07-21 |title=China starts building world's largest dam, fuelling fears in India |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c4gk1251w14o |access-date=2025-07-23 |website=www.bbc.com |language=en-GB}}</ref> granting it the ability to generate significant amounts of hydroelectric power. This section flows through the [[Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon]], recognized as Earth's deepest canyon system. The intended construction plan necessitates the excavation of four 20-kilometer tunnels through [[Namcha Barwa]] mountain to divert the Yarlung Tsangpo River.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=China to build world's largest hydropower dam in Tibet |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/crmn127kmr4o |access-date=2024-12-28 |website=www.bbc.com |date=27 December 2024 |language=en-GB}}</ref> A cascade of five hydropower stations is planned.<ref>{{Cite web |last=刘小卓 |title=Premier announces construction of Yarlung Zangbo hydropower project |url=https://www.chinadaily.com.cn/a/202507/19/WS687b6e94a310ad07b5d90d42.html |access-date=2025-08-18 |website=www.chinadaily.com.cn}}</ref>

== Impact on flow ==
According to Chinese officials, the dams being constructed on the Yarlung Tsangpo are of the [[Run-of-the-river hydroelectricity|run-of-the-river]] type, in which water is diverted through tunnels to a lower elevation to generate electricity and then returned to the river. Such systems do not store significant volumes of water for extended periods, unlike large reservoir-based dams capable of extensive flow regulation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Zhang |first=Hongzhou |last2=Donnellon-May |first2=Genevieve |date=2021-09-01 |title=China's Hydropower Plan on the Brahmaputra |url=https://thediplomat.com/2021/09/chinas-hydropower-plan-on-the-brahmaputra/ |journal=The Diplomat}}</ref><ref>{{citation |last=Asaduzzaman |first=Mohammad |title=The Strategic Ripples of China’s Mega-Dam for Bangladesh |date=2025-08-06 |magazine=The Diplomat |url=https://thediplomat.com/2025/08/the-strategic-ripples-of-chinas-mega-dam-for-bangladesh/ |id={{ProQuest|3237431314}}}}</ref>

Although the Yarlung Tsangpo originates inside Tibet, within Chinese borders, the majority of the Brahmaputra River's annual discharge (65–70%) is generated within India, primarily through monsoon rainfall and tributaries.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2025-06-06 |title=Hydrology of the Brahmaputra & implications of Chinese dam projects |url=https://striveedgeias.in/brahmaputra-hydrology-chinese-dam-impacts/ |access-date=2025-07-21 |website=Strive Edge IAS |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Tribune |first=The Assam |date=2025-06-03 |title='Brahmaputra fed by Indian rains': CM says reduced China flow may aid flood control |url=https://assamtribune.com/assam/brahmaputra-fed-by-indian-rains-cm-says-reduced-china-flow-may-aid-flood-control-1579744 |access-date=2025-07-21 |website=assamtribune.com |language=en}}</ref> Scientific studies also estimate that only about 25% of the river's total flow originates from snow and glacial melt in the upper Tibetan reaches.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Palash |first1=Wahid |last2=Bajracharya |first2=Sagar Ratna |last3=Shrestha |first3=Arun Bhakta |last4=Wahid |first4=Shahriar |last5=Hossain |first5=Md. Shahadat |last6=Mogumder |first6=Tarun Kanti |last7=Mazumder |first7=Liton Chandra |date=2023-01-05 |title=Climate Change Impacts on the Hydrology of the Brahmaputra River Basin |journal=Climate |language=en |volume=11 |issue=1 |pages=18 |bibcode=2023Clim...11...18P |doi=10.3390/cli11010018 |issn=2225-1154 |doi-access=free|hdl=2429/89920 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Due to this hydrological profile, upstream hydropower infrastructure, such as the Medog Hydropower Station, is expected to have a limited effect on downstream flows. [[Assam]] Chief Minister [[Himanta Biswa Sarma]] has remarked that the Brahmaputra is predominantly a rain-fed Indian river system, and has suggested that even if China were to reduce upstream flow, it might in fact potentially help mitigate the annual floods in Assam, which displace hundreds of thousands of people and destroy livelihoods.<ref>{{Cite news |last=PTI |date=2025-06-03 |title=After Indus Waters Treaty abeyance, Pakistan floating threat narrative of 'what if China stops Brahmaputra flow': Himanta |url=https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/after-indus-waters-treaty-abeyance-pakistan-floating-threat-narrative-of-what-if-china-stops-brahmaputra-flow-himanta/article69652039.ece |access-date=2025-07-21 |work=The Hindu |language=en-IN |issn=0971-751X}}</ref>

However, there have been raised concerns in India and Bangladesh, downstream nations that rely on the river. While China assures that the project will not impede water flow, India is concerned about potential impacts on water supply and flooding.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-04-28 |title=What would the world's largest dam mean for India and Bangladesh? |url=https://www.abc.net.au/asia/china-plans-to-build-world-largest-dam-india-bangladesh-impact/105223710 |access-date=2025-07-21 |website=ABC Asia |language=en-AU}}</ref>

== Criticism ==
The project has faced resistance from various parties, which include [[List of environmental organizations|environmental organizations]], downstream nations, and Tibetan rights groups. Similar hydroelectric developments in Tibet have previously sparked protests, including recent demonstrations against the Kamtok Dam project on the [[Yangtze|Drichu/Yangtze River]] that led to over 1,000 arrests. India and Bangladesh have also voiced apprehension about the project's potential effects on their water resources.<ref name=":0" />

CNN reported that Chinese leader [[Xi Jinping]] called for the project to be advanced "forcefully, systematically, and effectively" during a visit earlier in 2025 to Tibet.<ref name="cnn-20251217">{{Cite news |last1=McCarthy |first1=Simone |last2=Xiong |first2=Yong |date=2025-12-17 |title=China is building the world's most powerful hydropower system deep in the Himalayas. It remains shrouded in secrecy |url=https://edition.cnn.com/2025/12/17/china/china-largest-hydropower-dam-intl-hnk-dst |access-date=2025-12-19 |work=CNN}}</ref>

=== Cultural impact and displacement ===
{{Further|Chinese settlements in Tibet|Sinicization of Tibet}}
Tibetan rights organizations characterized the project as an example of [[Exploitation of natural resources|resource exploitation]] at the expense of [[Culture of Buddhism|Buddhist cultural heritage]] and local communities.<ref name=":2" />

While specific displacement figures remain undisclosed, the project will necessitate population relocation in the affected area. For comparison, the Three Gorges Dam project resulted in approximately 1.4 million relocations, although the Medog region's lower population density and absence of a reservoir suggest fewer displacements may be required. The development threatens to impact culturally significant sites in what Tibetans consider one of their most sacred regions. According to the [[International Campaign for Tibet]], the 193 combined projects in the region could potentially displace over 1.2 million people and affect numerous religious sites if completed.<ref>{{Cite web |date=17 February 2025 |title=How data deficiency is hindering hydro-diplomacy between China and India|url=https://india.mongabay.com/2025/02/commentary-how-data-deficiency-is-hindering-hydro-diplomacy-between-china-and-india/ |access-date=8 June 2025|language=en}}</ref>

The upcoming Medog hydropower station in Tibet has also raised concerns among the Adi tribal community in Arunachal Pradesh, India, who fear that the dam could significantly reduce water flow in the Siang River, threatening their traditional livelihoods and agricultural practices. Local leaders have warned that sudden releases of water from the dam could cause catastrophic flooding, endangering lives, property, and cultural heritage in the Siang belt, where the Adi and similar tribes reside.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |date=2025-07-21 |title=China starts building world's largest dam, fuelling fears in India |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c4gk1251w14o |access-date=2025-07-22 |website=www.bbc.com |language=en-GB}}</ref>

=== Environmental ===
Human rights groups have expressed concerns about the dam causing significant ecological damage to the region, one of the most diverse in the Tibetan Plateau.<ref name=":2" />

Environmental concerns have also been raised about the irreversible impact of dam construction in the Yarlung Tsangpo gorge, where the river descends 2,000 meters over a 50-kilometre span. The region includes a national nature reserve and is considered one of China's most important biodiversity hotspots.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |date=2025-07-22 |title=More power than Britain: China kick-starts mega dam to bolster economy |url=https://www.afr.com/world/asia/more-power-than-britain-china-kick-starts-mega-dam-to-bolster-economy-20250722-p5mgsh |access-date=2025-07-22 |website=Australian Financial Review |language=en}}</ref>

Dr. Jogendranath Sharma, a geologist, warned that the project, located in a seismically active region, poses serious risks to downstream Assam—including erosion, ecological disruption, and potential disaster in the event of an earthquake—urging a joint Indo-China environmental impact assessment.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Network |first=Hub |date=2025-06-30 |title=Mega dam threat: Expert warns of catastrophic impact on Assam from China's Medog Project |url=https://hubnetwork.in/mega-dam-threat-expert-warns-of-catastrophic-impact-on-assam-from-chinas-medog-project/ |access-date=2025-07-22 |website=Hub News |language=en-US}}</ref> The steep, narrow topography of the gorge caused geological experts to warn about increased landslide risks. In 2022, engineers from the Sichuan provincial geological bureau specifically highlighted the dangers of "earthquake-induced landslides and mud-rock flows" as significant threats to the project's stability.<ref name=":2" />

Aravind Yelery, associate professor at the Centre for East Asian Studies at [[Jawaharlal Nehru University]], stated that the dam could trap nutrient-rich sediments essential for soil fertility in downstream regions such as Assam and Bangladesh, potentially affecting irrigation. He added that the project may also reduce crop yields, harm agricultural productivity, and disrupt riverine ecosystems.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Should India worry about China's massive dam? – DW – 07/30/2025 |url=https://www.dw.com/en/should-india-worry-about-chinas-massive-dam/a-73465878 |access-date=2025-08-11 |website=dw.com |language=en}}</ref>

[[Mass media in China|Chinese state media]] has emphasised that the dam is a "a safe project that prioritises ecological protection", and stressed that it will boost the local economy and aid Beijing's climate neutrality goals, however, have not provided details on impact.<ref name=":2" />

In July 2026, the ''[[South China Morning Post]]'' reported that Chinese geologists had found an active Paizhen Fault beneath the planned Medog Hydropower Station as a major geological risk. The report said the fault could increase the risk of earthquakes, landslides, and slope failures, affecting the dam's structural stability.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |date=2026-07-11 |title=Chinese geologists warn of active fault line dangers from world’s largest hydropower project in Tibet |url=https://www.tibetanreview.net/chinese-geologists-warn-of-active-fault-line-dangers-from-worlds-largest-hydropower-project-in-tibet/ |access-date=2026-07-15 |website=[[Tibetan Review]] |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=July 13, 2026 |title=China's own geologists warn of active fault under Brahmaputra mega dam in Tibet |url=https://www.firstpost.com/world/chinas-own-study-warns-of-active-fault-beneath-brahmaputra-dam-site-in-tibet-ws-e-14030861.html}}</ref>

=== Water security ===
The project has generated apprehension among downstream nations regarding water security. [[Hydrology|Hydrological experts]] have drawn parallels with China's previous dam projects on the [[Mekong|Mekong River]], where upstream water control has been associated with increased drought frequency and severity in downstream regions over the past twenty years. Critics noted that India and Bangladesh could face compromised water access, biodiversity disruption, and riverbank erosion akin to those faced by [[Thailand]], [[Vietnam]], and [[Cambodia]] from earlier Chinese hydroelectric projects.<ref name=":0" />

A 2020 analysis by the [[Lowy Institute]] indicated that China's control over Tibetan Plateau rivers could potentially provide significant [[Geopolitics|geopolitical]] leverage over [[Economy of India|India's economy]].<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Singh |first1=Ameya P. |last2=Tembey |first2=Urvi |date=2020-07-23 |title=India-China relations and the geopolitics of water |url=https://www.lowyinstitute.org/the-interpreter/india-china-relations-geopolitics-water |access-date=2025-01-04 |website=Lowy Institute |language=en}}</ref> Indian authorities responded to the project by exploring countermeasures, including the potential development of their own large-scale hydroelectric dam and reservoir system to mitigate the dam's impacts. The [[Ministry of Foreign Affairs (China)|Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs]] asserted in 2020 that China maintains a "legitimate right" to dam the river, stating they have considered downstream effects in their planning.<ref name=":2" />

In 2025, India expressed renewed concerns over China's construction of the hydropower station on the Yarlung Tsangpo River in Tibet, citing potential risks to regional water security, environmental stability, and downstream livelihoods. Indian officials and experts warned that the project could affect river flows into India, particularly the Siang and Brahmaputra rivers, which are vital for millions in the northeastern states. The [[Ministry of External Affairs (India)|Ministry of External Affairs]] stated that the project was being closely monitored and urged China to ensure transparency and consultation with downstream countries. External Affairs Minister [[S. Jaishankar]] raised the issue during his visit to China in July 2025 for the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Foreign Ministers’ Meeting, also calling for the resumption of suspended hydrological data sharing.<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-08-11 |title=India voices concern over China's mega dam project on Yarlung Tsangpo in Tibet |url=https://www.firstpost.com/world/india-voices-concern-over-chinas-mega-dam-project-on-yarlung-tsangpo-in-tibet-13923209.html |access-date=2025-08-11 |website=Firstpost |language=en-us}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=2025-08-10 |title=India seeks transparency from China over construction of mega dam on River Brahmaputra |url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/india/india-seeks-transparency-from-china-over-construction-of-mega-dam-on-river-brahmaputra/articleshow/123219826.cms |access-date=2025-08-11 |work=The Times of India |issn=0971-8257}}</ref>

Bangladesh has expressed concerns over water security due to China's construction of the Motuo Hydropower Station, which flows downstream into Bangladesh as the [[Jamuna River (Bangladesh)|Jamuna River]]. In February 2025, Bangladeshi officials formally requested more information from Beijing, citing potential impacts on river flow, agriculture, and livelihoods in the densely populated delta region, which depends heavily on consistent water levels from transboundary rivers originating in Tibet.<ref name=":3" /> China describes the Medog Hydropower Station as a run-of-the-river project with no impact on downstream flow, but Bangladesh has sought technical transparency and hydrological data to verify this. Malik Fida Khan, head of the [[Centre for Environmental and Geographic Information Services|Center for Environmental and Geographic Information Services]], warned that disruptions to the Brahmaputra—source of 70 percent of dry-season flow in the Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna basin—could harm Bangladesh's water security. Sharif Jamil, coordinator of [[Riverkeeper]] Bangladesh, called the project “unilateral and geographically sensitive”, warning that a lack of consultation could result in ecological and socio-economic risks. If upstream interventions from China destabilize the natural flow, a professor from the [[University of Dhaka]] opines that Bangladesh's "climate-stressed water security" could collapse.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Strategic Ripples of China's Mega-Dam for Bangladesh |url=https://thediplomat.com/2025/08/the-strategic-ripples-of-chinas-mega-dam-for-bangladesh/ |access-date=2025-08-11 |website=thediplomat.com |language=en-US}}</ref> . Analysts have noted that the absence of a binding multilateral legal framework governing the river is itself a strategic choice. China has not ratified the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Non-Navigational Uses of International Watercourses, and has consistently declined to enter bilateral water-sharing agreements with downstream nations. One analysis argues that the asymmetry of power derived from controlling the headwaters is strategically more valuable to Beijing than any formal commitment would be, and that the dam does not create coercive capacity over downstream nations but structurally amplifies it.<ref>{{cite web |author=Elian Morvane |date=2026-03-19 |title=A Barragem Como Arma Sem Gatilho |url=https://arcananews.com/a-barragem-como-arma-sem-gatilho/ |access-date=2026-03-20 |website=Arcana News |language=pt}}</ref>

extract: The Medog Hydropower Station (Chinese: 墨脱水电站) or Motuo Hydropower Station is a planned 60,000 megawatt (MW) run-of-the-river hydroelectric dam project on a single stretch or valley of a river under development on the Yarlung Tsangpo river in Tibet Autonomous Region, China. It is of four cascade dams across the Yarlung Tsangpo River and five separate power stations  Upon completion, it will become the world's largest hydropower facility, with an anticipated annual power generation capacity of 10.8 PJ or 300 billion kilowatt-hours—triple that of the Three Gorges Dam. The Chinese government authorized the dam's construction in December 2024, with an estimated investment exceeding 1 trillion yuan (approximately US$137 billion). Construction officially began on 19 July 2025. The project is intended to be developed as a single-phase installation, with commercial operations planned for 2033.
